title: 1MW No. 326: What We Get Wrong About Staying in Touch
author: Greg McKeown
summary: In this 1-Minute Wednesday issue, Greg McKeown argues that connection is built through small signals of care rather than grand gestures. He opens with the penguin that carries a single pebble to its chosen mate, then borrows Vanessa Van Edwards's term 'pebbling' for small, thoughtful gestures like sending a meme or a two-line text asking how a presentation went. Citing a 2023 study by Peggy Liu and colleagues, he notes that people routinely underestimate how much a simple check-in will be appreciated, and that surprising messages are appreciated most. Most of us hold back because we think the message is too small to matter. He links pebbles to his earlier idea of life as loops that begin when something comes back, and closes with practical rhythms: follow up within three days of a meaningful conversation and check in every four to six weeks with friends you rarely see.
points: McKeown's core claim is that connection is sustained by small, frequent signals of care rather than grand gestures.
Pebbling, sending a meme or a short question about someone's big day, communicates that you noticed, remembered and cared.
Research cited from Liu and colleagues shows senders systematically underestimate how much a check-in message is appreciated, especially when it is surprising.
The barrier is our own assumption that a small message is an interruption, which the issue treats as being too hard on ourselves.
He offers concrete cadences: follow up within three days of a meaningful conversation and check in every four to six weeks with distant friends.
quotes: Connection is not built in grand gestures. It is built in small signals of care.
In her new book, Conversation, she turns this penguin ritual into a human practice called pebbling: small, thoughtful gestures that signal care.
Each one, she writes, carries the same message: "I noticed you. I remembered. I care.

In a 2023 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, researcher Peggy Liu and her colleagues found that people routinely underestimate how much a simple check-in message will be appreciated by the person receiving it.
Most of us hold back anyway. We assume our message is too small to matter, like it’s an interruption or noise that nobody wants to hear.
After a meaningful conversation, follow up within three days. For friends you rarely see, a small check-in every four to six weeks keeps the bond warm.
Pebbles don’t need to be a huge thing. Small is good. Small is caring.
